extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate mathematics students studying differential geometry / classical differential analysis (French reading)
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter-scale textbook guidance about types of curves on surfaces (lines of curvature, asymptotic lines, level/steepest‑descent lines, geodesics, conjugate directions) with definitions, necessary-and-sufficient conditions, differential equations, and worked examples. Includes a rule on differentiation under the integral sign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lines of curvature on a surface of revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: On a surface of revolution the lines of curvature are the parallels and the meridians; principal directions at a point are tangents to the meridian and to the parallel through the point, and the corresponding principal centers are: (1) the intersection C of the normal at the point with the axis of revolution; (2) the center of curvature of the meridian at the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: normals along a parallel form a cone with vertex on the axis (giving first family), normals along a meridian lie in the meridian plane and have an envelope equal to the evolute of the meridian (giving second family). Example: surface of revolution generated by a catenary—principal radii equal and opposite so mean curvature zero (minimal surface).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lines of curvature on a developable surface
rubrics_metrics.description: On a developable surface the lines of curvature consist of the straight generators and the curves orthogonal to those generators (the developantes of the edge of regression).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One principal radius is infinite at each point (generator direction), so Gaussian curvature is zero everywhere. Construction: trace the developable's generators (one family) and the orthogonal trajectories (second family) obtained by unwrapping a thread from the edge of regression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of asymptotic lines
rubrics_metrics.description: An asymptotic line on a surface is a curve whose tangent at each point is along one of the surface's asymptotic directions (directions in which normal curvature vanishes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asymptotic directions exist (are real) only where the Gaussian (total) curvature is negative or zero, so asymptotic lines exist only on parts of the surface with non‑positive Gaussian curvature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential equation for asymptotic lines (projection on xy‑plane)
rubrics_metrics.description: The horizontal projection of asymptotic lines has slope m = dy/dx satisfying the quadratic relation coming from the second derivatives of z: l m^2 + 2 m s + r = 0 (notation l, s, r are second partial derivatives), equivalently the second‑order differential equation (written in the text as (3) / (4)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This equation is quadratic in dy/dx; real roots (real directions) occur iff Gaussian curvature < 0. Integrating yields two families of asymptotic lines (one for each root). The text gives the explicit algebraic form and indicates how to eliminate denominators and reduce to an integrable form in examples (e.g., helicoid).

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymptotic lines on a ruled surface (surface réglée gauche)
rubrics_metrics.description: On a ruled surface one asymptotic direction at each point is the straight generator; the other asymptotic direction is necessarily real. Thus one system of asymptotic lines is formed by the straight generators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The second system consists of curves whose tangents at each point give the other asymptotic direction. Example: left helicoid—one family are generators projecting as straight lines through origin; the other family project to circles (yielding helices on the surface).

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymptotic lines on a developable surface
rubrics_metrics.description: On a developable surface the two asymptotic directions coincide (since one second derivative vanishes), so the two families of asymptotic lines reduce to the single family formed by the straight generators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequently asymptotic lines on developable surfaces are exactly the generators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of asymptotic lines (necessary and sufficient condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A curve on a surface is an asymptotic line iff at each of its points its osculating plane is tangent to the surface (equivalently the osculating plane coincides with the tangent plane of the surface at that point).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation: differentiate coordinate relations along the curve and impose the osculating‑plane conditions (vanishing of appropriate determinants); yields condition dp/ds + f... = 0 (text gives the differential form). Example: normals generated by principal normals of a space curve produce a ruled surface whose directrix curve is asymptotic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions: level lines (contours) and lines of greatest slope
rubrics_metrics.description: Level lines (lignes de niveau) are intersections of the surface with horizontal planes; their horizontal projections are given by F(x,y,C)=0 when the surface is F(x,y,z)=0. Lines of greatest slope are curves on the surface that cut the level lines orthogonally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projections of level lines are in true scale on the xy‑plane. Lines of greatest slope project to curves orthogonal to the projected level lines; these projected curves satisfy a first‑order differential equation derived from p and q (the partial derivatives ∂z/∂x and ∂z/∂y).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential equation for projections of lines of greatest slope
rubrics_metrics.description: The horizontal projection y(x) of a line of greatest slope satisfies a differential equation obtained from p dx + q dy = dz and orthogonality to level lines (where dz=0): the text derives equation (11)/(12) which one integrates when p,q are known (i.e., when z=f(x,y)) or uses implicit formulas when surface given by F(x,y,z)=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When z is solved as z=f(x,y) the quantities p and q are explicit functions of x and y and the ODE can be integrated. If the surface is given implicitly, use relations (N° 184) for p and q in terms of F and include z as function of x,y via the surface equation, then integrate the resulting ODE. Example: ellipsoid case integrates to curves y = A x^m (variables separable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lines of greatest slope are orthogonal to level lines (projection property)
rubrics_metrics.description: The horizontal projections of lines of greatest slope meet at right angles the horizontal projections of level lines; equivalently, in the xy‑plane, the lines with slopes given satisfy the orthogonality relation derived in equation (10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric reason: in space the right angle between level line and steepest‑descent line has one side parallel to the projection plane, so the projected angle is right; analytic reason: from p dx + q dy = 0 along level lines and the orthogonality condition one obtains the differential relation in the plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geodesics: definition and variational/geometric characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: A geodesic on a surface is a curve whose osculating plane at each point is normal to the surface (equivalently, the principal normal to the curve coincides with the surface normal). Geodesics are the locally shortest paths on the surface (they are stationary/minimizing for length among nearby curves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanical model: a taut frictionless string on the surface assumes an equilibrium curve which is a geodesic. A geodesic joining two points may be a local minimum (stable equilibrium) or an unstable one; not every geodesic between two points is globally shortest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of geodesics on standard surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Plane: geodesics are straight lines. Sphere: geodesics are great circles (their osculating plane contains the sphere's normal). Cylinder: geodesics are helices (developing the cylinder turns them into straight lines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remarks: on a sphere between two points there can be two geodesics (shorter and longer arcs of great circle) corresponding to stable/unstable equilibria; on cylinders there exist infinitely many geodesics between two points if the cross‑section is closed (wraps produce many development straight lines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geodesics on developable surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon developing a developable surface onto the plane, geodesics map to straight lines; thus geodesics on a developable surface are exactly those curves which develop to straight lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use: to find geodesics on a developable, develop the surface and draw straight lines between corresponding developed points; inverse map gives geodesics on the surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invariance of geodesics under bending (isometric deformations)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a surface is considered as a flexible but inextensible fabric, geodesics drawn on it are preserved under any bending (isometric deformation) of the fabric: lines that are locally shortest remain locally shortest after deformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence of inextensibility: lengths and angles along the fabric remain unchanged, so geodesic property is invariant under such deformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geodesic curvature and expression via projection
rubrics_metrics.description: The geodesic radius of curvature at a point of a curve on a surface equals the radius of curvature of the projection of that curve onto the tangent plane at the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical formula: compute the curve's projection onto the tangent plane at the point and take its curvature/radius there to obtain the geodesic curvature/radius. The text also relates the space curvature, the angle between the osculating plane and tangent plane, and the geodesic radius (points of development inflection are characterized accordingly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Points of inflection of the development
rubrics_metrics.description: Points of inflection in the planar development correspond to points where the planar curvature p' is infinite, equivalently either (1) the osculating plane of the curve is normal to the developable surface (angle O = π/2), or (2) the space curve itself has infinite radius of curvature (straight inflection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these criteria to detect inflection points when developing a curve from a surface to the plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directions conjugate and conjugate nets
rubrics_metrics.description: Two directions in the tangent plane at a point are conjugate if they are conjugate diameters of the indicatrix at that point; two families of curves form a conjugate net if at each point the tangent directions to the two families are conjugate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: principal directions are conjugate; lines of curvature form a conjugate net. This is used in the theorem of conjugate tangents and in shadowing/characteristic constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem of conjugate tangents (characteristic generator direction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a curve C on a surface, the moving tangent plane along C envelops a developable whose characteristic generator AG at a point A has direction conjugate to the tangent AT to C at A (i.e., AG is the conjugate direction of AT in the tangent plane).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch: write tangent plane equation depending on parameter, differentiate, obtain the characteristic by eliminating the parameter; in principal directions coordinates the characteristic is the conjugate diameter of the indicatrix. Application: used constantly in theory of caustics / shadow lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for differentiation under the integral sign (constant limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: If I(A) = ∫_a^b f(x,A) dx with integrand f depending on parameter A and fixed limits a,b (independent of A), then dI/dA = ∫_a^b ∂f(x,A)/∂A dx, provided the resulting integral exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation via increment and limit of difference quotient is given. The rule can be iterated for higher derivatives under the integral sign when integrals remain well‑defined; used to derive new integrals from known ones (example begins afterwards).
